Mr. Speaker, may I give an oral answer to this question? The same question is asked almost every session, although the answer is very clear. The Military Service Act, 1917, is spent. It ceased to be in force after demobilization, following the conclusion of the war and the completion and fulfilment of the consequential provisions of the act. Had this item passed I would not have had a word to say about it. I am not condemning the minister for reducing the item by $10,000 because I assume the explanation is that there is no demand from the public schools for the money. I should be delighted to see the minister increase the grant by $500,000, if for no other reason than to assist private schools and colleges. Take, for instance, the De la Salle organization and St. Andrew's College in Toronto, two of the best drilled corps in this country, equal almost to the Kingston cadets. The cadet services should be encouraged, and if the public schools do not want the money let the private schools in any part of this country have it. The militia regiments should also get a little more money to encourage them to have a cadet corps in connection with every regiment. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that cadet training should be encouraged because it is the sort of training that makes men out of the boys. To see them on parade is a beautiful sight, and everyone who sees them applauds them. Where were the instructors located, what amount was paid to each of them, and what are their names?
Sanderson, A. R., $2,153.50; Cummings, W., of the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, $1,642.50; and Joyner, C., of the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, $1,916.25.
Were there any travelling expenses in addition?

Yes.
They are included in these total estimates. They are not shown individually.
How many corps would they inspect, and where were the corps located?
I understand that twenty-eight units is the total in Saskatchewan, and between the three instructors they would, I assume, all be inspected.
I just wondered how many days were occupied in inspecting these cadet corps.

I cannot answer that. When the instructors were not discharging this particular duty they would be engaged in other work whether for cadets or district headquarters.

I may tell the minister that when they inspect corps in the cities they can hold six or seven inspections a day. Some hon. member says they can do no such thing, but I know that an inspection in my institution used to last about three-quarters of an hour one day a year, so I know precisely what I ana 'talking about. Whait I am trying to point out is that in my opinion this grant is a wasteful one, that if it is to be used for physical training we could use it to much better advantage in another connection. I am objecting to 'the expenditure not only on the ground of military training but in the public interest on the ground of wastefulness, because I am convinced from my own experience that as used now it is a wasteful expenditure.

I agree to a certain extent with what was said by the hon. member who has just spoken. If this vote is not for military purposes, I do not see why it should not be transferred to the Department of Pensions and National Health.
Could we have the location of these twentyjeight corps in Saskatchewan?
I have not that information with me, but I shall be glad to get it for the hon. member.
From what parts of Canada have requests for grants ceased to come?

The
decreases in cadet detachments are: Alberta, three; British Columbia, one; Nova Scotia, five; Ontario, seventeen; Prince Edward Island, one; Quebec, twenty-five; Saskatchewan, eight; Manitoha, two, or a total of sixty-two detachments.
Those are discontinued?
Yes.

Is Mr. Sanderson the physical training instructor in the Regina normal school, and is this payment really for the work he does there? I may say that the work Mr. Sanderson is doing in that institution is excellent, but it is not only military work. I think that point should be made clear.

I am unable to answer the hon. member's question. The instructor is shown here as "sergeant-major instructor A. R. Sanderson of the R.C.R." My hon. friend will probably know better than I whether Mr. Sanderson is doing other things as well.

Have there been any
increases in units, and if so in what provinces?
Yes, in three provinces: New Brunswick, one; Ontario, one; Saskatchewan, one.

The fact that seventy-two units throughout Canada have been disbanded-
Mr.	MACKENZIE	(Vancouver):	Sixtytwo detachments.Miss	MACPHAIL:	I think the	minister
said seventy-two-that sixty-two units have been disbanded throughout Canada goes to show that there is a lack of interest in cadet training. I have many times carefully argued the matter. I do not think that this is good physical training, and if it is military training it would be better that it should be definitely military training in one of the military units. This vote, it seems to me, comes in between those two positions, and it would be well to get rid of it as soon as possible. I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Coldwell:
That item 60 in the estimates be reduced by $139,999.

Speaking to the amendment, some years ago I supported the view of the hon. member for Grey-Bruce when she moved a reduction of a similar item. At that time I said that I was ready to support her in order that the vote should be set at a reasonable figure. It seems to me that it is now nearer that level, although not precisely so, because it should be $150,000. At the time we protested against the vote it was several hundreds of thousands of dollars, but it is now much less. I regret not to be able to support the amendment moved by our charming colleague. On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that every member would approve of the transference of that vote to the Department of Pensions and National Health, if the purpose of the vote is what it is said to be, and were that done, I am sure the hon. member for Grey-Bruce would withdraw her motion.

In my opinion the hon. member for Temiscouata gave the best reason why this vote should be eliminated: he intimated that a few years ago it amounted

to $700,000 and that it is now down to $140,000. If there were any great demand in the country for this service, there is no doubt that hon. members would be receiving letters and resolutions asking them to support a larger grant. But all the resolutions and all the letters we get are in opposition to any grant whatever.
No, no.
The hon. member for Parkdale says "No, no."
I did not say "no, no," but I will do so now.

That reminds me that when he suggested that this grant or an increased grant be given to any school, public or private, that requested it, he was on very dangerous ground, because if grants are to be made to private schools there will soon be received sufficient applications from such schools to absorb a very much larger vote than this, and one could have no assurance that the money would be used to the advantage of the people of this country. There is a considerable demand throughout Canada for physical training; it is something that has been neglected for a great many years. To say that this grant is given for physical training is foolish. This instruction is not physical training; it continues for a very short period in the year, in fact for only a few months, whereas the children are in school for ten months. If we are to have physical training it should be given over the ten months during which children are in school. If the federal government wishes to contribute to physical training it can do so in a much better way and one that would be much more beneficial to the various municipalities who have difficulty in finding money for school needs. It can be done much more satisfactorily than by means of this grant, which is not required or needed. If it were not a free gift from the government there is not a school in the west that would accept it.

I wish to make a few observations in sppport of this vote, or at all events of the minister's intentions. I said the other night that I was sorry to see the vote cut down, but the minister's explanation was satisfactory and I wish to express my approval. I have had something to do with cadet training but it seems to me that the cadet training with which I am acquainted is something different from what my hon. friend (Mr. Coldwell) has been discussing. Instead of training for two months the cadets that I am speaking of receive training throughout the year. Every week in the twelve months they are thoroughly trained. I am now
referring to the sea cadet corps at Halifax and in all the principal cities of the country. In Quebec and Montreal there are splendid corps; I have seen the cadets in Ottawa, and I have seen them in Toronto and in Oshawa. There is a splendid corps in Winnipeg. I am not so sure about Regina. My hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar tells me that there is one there. I know that there used to be one and I am glad to hear that it is still there. I know there is a fine corps in Vancouver.
These cadets are given thorough physical training every week and are taught a great many things that will stand them in excellent stead as they go along in life. I sometimes go to see them train and I know they are taught all sorts of useful vocations in connection with cadet work and so on, all of which makes them real men. I am proud of the work that is done for young Canadians by the cadet corps with which I am associated. These particular cadets are also trained in connection with shipping. I have not by me at the moment the number of Canadian boys trained in the cadet corps supported by the Department of National Defence under this vote and now serving on ships throughout the world. I believe the boys are sent from Toronto to the ship Conway in England and are there given excellent training, graduating to the merchant marine. I know of a large number of young Canadians who are now serving on ships of the empire-not particularly warships, though I see no reason why they could not graduate to that branch of naval service. I am speaking of cadets that finally go on merchant ships. The Canadian Pacific and other shipping companies have them.
This is good work the department is doing for Canada and I like to see these young men trained. They are altogether different from the young fellows one sees standing around the street corners. I have not an unkind word to say about the boys that stand around street corners because they have not the same opportunities that you and I had when we were boys; and if the minister had double the appropriation he could train a good many more boys and take them off the corners in the evenings.
When I go to the Navy League headquarters on the lake shore in Toronto I see there in training, on Tuesday nights, I believe, anywhere from a hundred to a hundred and fifty of these boys, and it is interesting to watch them. They are taught civility; they are encouraged to think quickly and to be prompt in action and in formations. And that is what the young folk want to do instead of standing around the street corners
Supply-Defence-Cadets

learning nothing. I am not so familiar now with what goes on in the schools and I cannot speak from experience, but I know that in 1936 the physical instructor of the collegiate institute in Belleville-I believe his name is James Willis Howard gave a fine discourse to Ithaca university in New York on the value of cadet training. It was so well thought of that it was quoted in Ameri-man newspapers and journals throughout the country. That is one physical instructor in a collegiate institute in Canada who fully endorses this movement. It is with great pleasure that I shall vote against the amendment when it is submitted to the committee.

Before the vote is taken on the amendment may I ask the minister whether he is prepared to consider transferring this vote from his department to the Department of Health? If the Minister of Pensions and National Health is not ready to consider taking over this item in his own department-
That's just as bad.

May I tell the hon. member for Parkdale, after the interesting speech just delivered by the hon. member for Davenport with regard to the health of the boys who receive special training under the Department of National Defence, that these healthy boys should be transferred to the Department of National Health so as to keep up the name of that department; otherwise if they are all sick there, we shall have to sail it the Department of Sickness.

It is certainly not my intention to say much this year on the subject before us. I am able to speak from experience as to what cadet training does. In the Yukon in the very early days we had a cadet corps taken charge of voluntarily by an officer of what was then known as the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and the boys in the city of Dawson at that time fairly scrambled over one another to get into that little corps. It was an honour to join and be kept on and a decided dishonour when a boy was let out. It trained the boys mentally, physically and morally. As I say, I can only speak from experience, having had three boys disciplined in that way-a very small number; I should have had more. It is interesting to me to know that the school cadet movement, the object of which is to impart mental, moral and physical training to the youth of Canada and to develop in them the principles of patriotism and good citizenship, was first authorized by an amendment to the Militia Act for the province of Canada, assented to at

Quebec on June 9, 1862, under which authority was granted for the formation of associations, for purposes of drill in universities and schools. Enrolment in a school cadet corps, in so far as the department is concerned, is a purely voluntary matter on the part of the individual school boy. During the past summer twenty-nine cadet corps held private camps for their members, without expense to the government, receiving on loan from the department various articles of camp equipment. Under the provisions of the Strathcona trust and in accordance with an agreement entered into by the Department of Militia and various provincial educational authorities the Department of Militia agreed to supply qualified physical training instructors for duty at normal schools.
I do not see how anyone who watches the boys of the present day, out of work, with very little to amuse them and in many cases, no money, can possibly object to this cadet training. The boys in this country, the children in this country, need more and more every day mental, moral and physical training. By joining the cadet corps they are brought in touch with people who are interested in the youth of the country, and if we do not bring up the youth of the country as we ought, what is going to happen in the future?

I am afraid that several things are being confused. No one is objecting to physical culture. Indeed I should like to see a much larger grant for physical training. But I am pointing out that cadet drill is not the best kind of physical culture. In fact most of the progressive countries of Europe, including the old land, have to a very large extent abandoned cadet training. Cadet training is military training, not physical training. You can if you wish give physical training in small doses, but I think all the drill sergeant's idea is to get a number of boys out on parade and see how quickly they can obey him without thinking particularly of what they are doing.
Theirs not to reason why,
Theirs but to do and die.
On the other hand physical training should make a child alert and well balanced physically. If you want to make a grant for physical training, of which I am thoroughly in favour, then I suggest it be taken from under the Department of Defence and placed under the Department of Health or the educational departments of the several provinces. Then we could adopt modem systems of physical education.

________________Supply-Defence-Cadets
There is no one in this committee more interested in physical education than I am. I have taken a great deal of it myself and have given a great deal from time to time. The poorest form of physical training is the kind that is given in cadet corps. If we want to continue to pay $5,000 a year for the supervision of twelve hundred cadets in Saskatchewan, when that money could be scattered over a large number of schools to aid in giving physical education, well and good; but in my opinion this country cannot afford to spend money wastefully. I would rather see $1,000,000 spent efficiently than this $140,000 spent, as I regard it, wastefully. I am not saying that the men in charge of this work are not doing their best; they are. But the system under which they work is in my opinion wrong. We should consider more modern methods of giving organized supervised games and physical education.
The hon. member for Davenport spoke of the naval cadets. I doubt whether naval cadets are included in this appropriation.
Sea cadets are.

He tells us it is much better to have the boys drilling in the evening than standing around the street corners. But let me point out that in all the cases of which I have knowledge the training is given not in the evenings but during school hours, usually at the close of the school day. It does not take anyone off the streets; all it does is to take a group of boys out of their regular classes for a certain length of time. If we are to make a grant for physical training let it be for physical training, and let it be for girls as well as for boys, and then we can get it under the department of health. Followed to its logical conclusion, the argument we have had this afternoon would simply mean that what we ought to do is to put everyone in military uniform and give him physical training. Then indeed we should have a situation comparable to that in Germany and Italy under Hitler and Mussolini.

I did not intend to say anything with reference to this matter, but some arguments have been brought up with which I do not entirely agree. I had some experience in cadet work as inspector of schools for a number of years in New Brunswick and I must say that my experience was that wherever you found a cadet corps in a school you always found a school where the discipline was good, the physical training good and the children more alert than in other schools. Cadet training is physical training, and the very best physical training. Physical
training of course comes entirely under the school curriculum, and the school curriculum, as we know, is made up by the educational department for the different schools. As to military training, as militia officer in the past I have found that young men coming in from the towns and country districts after even ten or fifteen days in a militia camp show a great improvement in smartness and the way they carry themselves. I do not think that either military training or cadet training hurts anyone. Those who had experience with men coming in from all sections of the country in the early days of the war must have observed the great improvement in physique after a short period of training. I am sure we cannot estimate in money the value to the young men of the Dominion of Canada of the training for which this money is voted. I am very much in favour of it. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says it teaches men to move automatically; my experience is that it teaches them to think quickly, makes their minds more alert. I make these few remarks because I believe in this kind of training and regard it as a great asset to the young manhood of Canada.

There has been much stress laid on making minds alert. If that is a result of cadet training, it might be a good idea to have a corps from the membership of the house on the grounds in front of this building. Much of what was said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar expresses what I would say in regard to the speech made by the hon. member for Davenport. He talked a great deal about getting the boys in uniform and off the street corners-
Pardon me; I did not mention the word uniform.

Well, the hon. member told us how smart they looked in their uniforms as he saw them being paraded, so that they must have had the uniforms on. I think we ought to be careful about that, because some people get so enthusiastic about getting boys in uniform, as in Germany and Italy for example, that they have got it down to little chaps about ten years of age. They get everyone into uniform and then say that they are curing unemployment. But getting people into uniform does not mean that the real problems of unemployment have been solved.
Many who have spoken have argued that cadet training makes boys more alert and quick to meet the problems of life. I think world 'authorities are agreed that it does not do that. The Last speaker (Mr. Brooks) referred to the change in the physique of men
Supply-Defence-Cadets

trained at the beginning of the war, but that was not all due to cadet training. A great deal of it was due to physical training, as every one knows, because cadet training is not good physical training. In order to have the men in good physical condition, physical training, which had nothing to do with cadet drill, had to be added.
I have said all I intend to say this year or other years. The vote should be transferred to the Department of National Health, or to the department of education, where it could be used for purposes of physical training, in which case it could be made much larger than it is to-day, and we could have training not only of boys, but of girls as well. If we are !to have physical training there is no reason why we Should take one part of the human race and train it to be physically fit, leaving the other part untrained. I shall continue to move that it be reduced until, some day, we will come to that conclusion.

I do not wish to talk at cross purposes. All hon. members want some type of training which will make our young people as healthy as possible, and make it possible for them to have exercise and physical development. We are trying to decide the best method of accomplishing that end, and upon that subject there seems to be some difference of opinion. I believe the figures the minister gave on Friday evening afford the best contradiction of what has been said by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and others.
The hon. member for Davenport is experienced in this.

For a number of years I was a member of a cadet corps, and from first-hand information I think I know something about cadets. From the very fact that sixty-two units have ceased to exist during the year it is apparent that cadet training no longer appeals to youth. Surely the hon. member for Davenport does not suggest that, because there are two and a half times as many cadets in the province of Quebec as there are in Ontario, there are two and a half times as many healthy boys.
There is not so much socialism and communism in Quebec.
I think we ought to keep to the subject.
Question.

I do not propose to be intimidated by hon. members shouting " question." The fact remains that the young boys are not accepting this type of training

as they used to; they are going into boy scout work and the Canadian standard efficiency tests.
What is that?

When the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) introduced his resolution suggesting a ministry of sports, and the Minister of National Health replied, it was the general consensus of opinion that there was room in Canada for some organized type of physical training and recreation, and that it should come under the departments of education in the provinces. This parliament could make grants to the provinces for that purpose. I should like to join with hon. members who have preceded me in saying that the vote should be transferred to the Department of National Health, with amounts allocated to the respective provinces to carry on cultural and physical training for the improvement of the youth of Canada. It should not be associated with the Department of National Defence, as it 'has been in the past.
What does the Minister of National Health think about the transfer of the vote? I ask him in the mildest manner if he will kindly give his answer to that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not know that I should object strenuously to having this branch of the Department of National Defence transferred to the Department of National Health. Of course, if parliament decides that it shall be done, there is nothing to do but to obey. But before undertaking any such task we would have to ask very large subsidies to provide for staff, instructors and other people who would undertake to carry out the training of the cadets. That is not so simple or easy as it would appear to the hon. member for Temiscouata. It is not practicable in one day to transfer from one department to another a branch of training which has been carried on for many years. I am sure that in any case nothing could be done this year, but I am willing to tell the hon. member for Temiscouata and other hon. members who have been so kind as to be willing to give me further responsibility, that during the interval between this session and the next I shall be only too pleased to study the possibilities of the situation.

I do not agree with the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) or the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) much as I should like to at times. Sometimes the hon. member for Grey-Bruce makes

Supply-Defence-Cadets
a very pleasant speech, and I feel like supporting her. However on this particular occasion may I say she has always had a hatred of cadet corps, and always shows a desire to reduce the vote. I am not blaming her for her attitude, but I must endorse the sentiments expressed by the hon. members for Yukon (Mrs. Black) and Royal (Mr. Brooks), who have had considerable experience. Why hon. members around me persist in saying there is no physical training in cadet corps work I cannot understand, because that is absolute rot. The cadet corps in Toronto about which I speak-and I assume they are the same in Vancouver, Winnipeg, and other large cities-shows evidence of physical training. Watching them passing on the street one can tell distinctly that they are well trained physically, or they would not be in the condition they are. Hon. members talk about training for ten days or two weeks. May I say that the boys in St. Andrew's College and De La Salle are training all the time; otherwise they would not be in such good condition.

Mr. Chairman, I was
a cadet instructor for nine years, and I believe I should know something about cadet work. At the same time I feel there is a belief on the part of people in the different provinces that the cadet instruction should be entirely revolutionized. Military training or regimentation as it has been practised in the past leads to only one or two good effects. So far as I can ascertain, the ability to think rapidly is not developed by cadet training. It is developed more readily by organized sports than by the regimentation brought about through cadet training.
The best feature in connection with cadet training, as I have known it, is that it encourages leadership. Cadet instructors, corps commanders and platoon commanders develop the ability to lead. Although this principle may be found in boy scout training, I should like to see it remain in the cadet movement. On the other hand I believe the principle under which cadet corps are organized is entirely wrong, because the municipalities and school boards need that money. The corps of which I was instructor happened three years in succession to win the shield given by the right hon. leader of the opposition. The members of the corps were mostly of Ukrainian parentage. It is said that people of that race make the most disciplined soldiers, although of that I am not certain. Napoleon once said that the Czechs were the best soldiers, because they were willing to
obey. No doubt the same conditions exist in some of the central European countries. I should like to see increased facilities provided for the development of the cadet idea. I am against the reduction in this amount, in fact I should like to see it raised to SI,900,000. If cadet training cannot be placed under the department of health this year, perhaps consideration will be given to this matter. The town in which I live was not able to provide any money for sports and we used the cadet money for that purpose. To-day the sports activities of the town have suffered considerably because the cadet corps has been disbanded and no more money is coming in for that purpose. I should like to see this vote increased to SI,000,000 in order that grants could be made to each of the provinces which in turn could divide up the money for the purpose of providing facilities for sport in the different towns and villages by which health and physique of the young people, both male and female, could be improved and developed.
Some one said that cadet training is the poorest form of physical training there is. I suppose he was referring to the mere handling of rifles and so on, but that is something that can be learned by any man who wants to be a soldier, in two weeks. To do that requires no mental discipline or cadet training. Many of our young men have no facilities by which they can develop themselves along mechanical lines. Many of these boys would like to be aeroplane mechanics as they have no liking for ordinary regimentation. A new and better outlook by society would lead to a cleaner and saner world.

I have given a good deal of attention to these cadet corps and I have come to tire conclusion that they are obsolete. I think we should pay more attention to providing proper methods of physical training for our young people, to be carried on under the direction of those who have taken advantage of the world's experience in this regard. I believe the results obtained would be much better as far as the physical and mental development of our young people is concerned. We should not be spending this amount to carry on physical and military training which is obsolete and merely a disguised form of recruiting for the military units. Facilities are needed everywhere for vocational and technical training which would prove of infinitely more value to our younger generation. My chief objection to this vote is the fact that it does not reach the young men who need it most. The benefits of this vote reach only a comparatively small number of young men, and I agree thoroughly with
Supply-Defence-C ade ts

the views expressed by the lien, member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that this money is wasted.
Amendment (Miss Macphail) negatived: yeas, 11; nays, 85.
Am I right in understanding that this vote covers the naval cadets?
Yes, the sea cadets.

I am a very strong supporter of these sea cadets. There is a corps in my city with which I have been intimately connected for many years and I am very grateful for the good work which has been done. It is gratifying to see the characters of these boys being moulded by the instructors and the petty officers. This work has been going on for several years and good results are being obtained. It is not a very easy thing to do when you are located three or four hundred miles from the coast, but we have been able to get some of these boys placed in the marine service. As far as the boys in the corps at Vancouver and the ports on the Atlantic coast are concerned, they are practically all absorbed into the merchant service and itheir record has been very good indeed. About half a dozen years ago it was necessary to reduce this vote almost to the vanishing point, and I should like to have the minister tell the committee to what extent these grants are now being made to the sea cadets, and whether he will consider increasing them.

The sea cadets are on exactly the same footing as the other cadet corps. Fourteen corps are affiliated with and six are not affiliated with the division of 'the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve.

When this vote was first brought before the committee I asked the minister a question with regard to supervision over the grants, and the minister explained that these grants were properly looked after by the department. However, after listening to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hayhurst) I am inclined to think 'that something must be wrong somewhere when the money supposed to go to the cadets has been spent for the purposes of sport and other recreational facilities. I should like to know how these funds are being used in other parts of the country and I am just wondering whether something should not be done to provide proper supervision and inspection. Perhaps the people in other districts could be given t'he same latitude in spending this

money as apparently has been given to the people in the district of 'the hon. member who spoke a few moments ago.
I can speak from knowledge of one officer who trained a corps, and I know that every cent he earned was used for the purchase of boxing gloves and footballs which he provided with his own money.

I should like to clear up this question of where the money went. The cadet instructor is supposed to put most of it in his own pocket, but in this particular case he gave it for the benefit of the community.

In connection with the sea cadet work, have any representations been made to the minister or the department in connection with an extension of this work? I know something about cadet work myself, and I know there are many limitations. Is the money paid to instructors in sea cadet work the same as is done in connection with the land cadet services?
Yes.

Has any thought been given by those in charge of the sea cadet services that the service might be extended a little to make it more interesting to the boys and develop them a little more? It provides one of the most marvellous trainings in the country, and I was wondering if the minister had received representations for an extension of this work, and if so, will he give them his serious consideration?

Numerous representations have been received praising the work carried out by the sea cadets. Very recently representations were made for an extension of this work, particularly on our coasts. Private citizens have made very strong representations to the department in that regard.
The minister gave the number of cadets by provinces for 1936. Could he give us the amount that was spent in each province?
It has not been broken down in that way.
It is not available by provinces?
No.
Is any training still given in marksmanship in any cadet corps?

Yes.

What type of institutions are qualified for assistance on account of marksmanship? Are instructions in marksmanship given under the supervision of militia units or under the cadet instructor attached to the school?
The instruction is given by the instructor who receives pay for these services, just as for the ordinary training of cadets.
Are the rifles and ammunition supplied by the department from assistance given for instruction purposes?
Rifles are issued and ammunition is supplied by the department.
The sea cadets vote would not in any sense cover the training in the ship that is being built down in Nova Scotia?
No.
Nothing to do with this vote?
No. That ship will not be finished until towards the end of this fiscal year.
That will not be covered by this vote?
Not under this vote at all.

Item agreed to.
Contingencies, $28,800.
Is there anything here about the pensions being paid to General McNaughton and Colonel Steel?

Not
under this vote.
Would the minister explain this vote?

This vote is to provide for the cost of telegrams and telephone calls, postage, and so forth for militia services at headquarters. It includes guards of honour and the expenses of the Bisley team, the latter item being estimated at $1,200.
What did guards of honour cost last year?
So far this year, $3,244.75.
In order to save time, may I ask the minister which is the item relating to the McNaughton and Steel stuff?

The pension is purely statutory under the terms of the Militia Pensions Act. I forget the exact section, but it is the one dealing with officers seconded from the Department of National Defence to any other department.

I wonder if I shall have to block all the estimates in order to get some information about these fellows. I understand the pension is statutory, but the money must be provided somewhere in the estimates like every other statutory expense.
Such pensions are payable by the Department of Pen sions.

Then the whole law should be repealed.

The minister, sipeaking in the house last week, stressed time and again the necessity for defending our ports and harbours. May I ask what provision is being made for the defence of our ports on the Pacific such as Prince Rupert, Victoria, Vancouver, New Westminster, and Alberni?

I think it would be better to answer that question in detail when we come to the various items, rather than make a general answer. Except

Only revotes.

Mr. Chairman, for the
very reasons which I have set forth during the debate on the amendment presented by the hon. member for Vancouver-North (Mr. MacNeil), I intend to oppose this increase in the National Defence estimates, and therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lacroix):
That item 62 of the National Defence estimates be reduced by $1,867,850.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lacroix) whether he wishes to eliminate the items concerning Valcartier, which are included in this vote?

I may point out to the
hon. member that this is not a matter of patronage, but of principle.
That argument should be conclusive.

The minister has stated that the estimates were, first, for the maintenance of internal security and the preservation of law and order within our territory, and second, for protection against any exterior aggression. Is the minister able to say what portion of these estimates is for the maintenance of internal security and the preservation of law and order within our territory, and what portion is for protection against any exterior aggression?

I am
afraid that is a very difficult question to answer to-day, but every cent of these estimates is to be used for the inside defence of the Dominion of Canada. As I stated in the main debate, it is not the intention to use any of these amounts for any purpose outside of the Dominion of Canada. That is as clear as I can possibly make it. This particular increase of $1,867,850 which we are now discussing is all for absolutely necessary
purposes within the Dominion of Canada, to try to make efficient the very small militia force we now have.
Some of the material will have to be bought outside of Canada, Mr. Chairman.
Yes, but very little of this vote provides for buildings and works.

I understand the minister to say it is for the defence of Canada, but it may be important to know where is our first line of defence. In view of the declaration made in the other chamber that our first line of defence is in Europe, may I ask the minister if he believes that our first line of defence is in Canada or in Europe?

That, Mr. Chairman, is a question of major policy, and possibly the hon. member is asking me concerning something that really should belong to the Prime Minister and the government as a whole. I believe it became very clear during the course of the debate last week that all the amounts asked for at this time in this vote are for the protection of Canadian territory or Canadian territorial waters, and under the items referred to in that debate there was no consideration of using any of this money for extraneous commitments or enterprises of any kind. I think that was made abundantly clear in the debate of a week ago. As to where the front line of Canada's defence is, I doubt if anybody here can with accuracy forecast. All I can say is that all the items in these estimates are intended only for the protection of Canada, of Canadian neutrality and of the territorial waters adjacent to our coast.
In other countries expenditures for similar purposes are spread over so many years. Has the minister anything of the kind in view here, or are these expenditures only for ;his year's program.
That is correct.
This does not contemplate anything in the future.
No; no specific plans have been laid down for next year. The estimates for any subsequent year will depend upon the conditions existing at that time, but no plans have been prepared for next year.

And can we expect that next year the estimates will be about the same as they were last year.

Supply-Defence-Engineers
The estimates next year will depend on the conditions prevailing in the world at that time.
Of the total increase more than half is for the defence of Vancouver?
Not Vancouver, but the Pacific coast.

I have no doubt the matter was given very serious consideration before the increases were made, but what expert opinion was obtained, and was the defence program for Vancouver decided upon as the most efficient that could be devised?

Very
careful consideration was given to the general plan arrived at in this connection. Perhaps I had better give some details with regard to this item of $805,000. This item is for the first stage of construction of emplacements, observation posts, defence light emplacements, power house, et cetera, in the vicinity of Esquimalt, Victoria, Vancouver, off Johnstone strait and off Prince Rupert. It will provide for the acquisition of property and for suffi-cent construction work to enable protection guns and other equipment to be mounted in case of necessity. It does not provide full protection and accommodation. The total estimated cost of the works contemplated would be about double the amount asked for this year.

If that is so, am I right in saying that these estimates, so far as the Pacific coast is concerned, are only a prelude to estimates of a similar kind to be brought down next year and the year following and for many more years to come?

That is not correct. It would probably mean that the same amount might be asked for next year, because $895,000 is roughly speaking about half the amount estimated as necessary for the particular purpose.
How much of that is for the protection of the lower mainland in British Columbia?

It is all designed for the same purpose; the protection of Vancouver island is not separated from the rest. It is all one coordinated plan of defence worked out by experts of the department and by others whose advice they have taken. I do not believe the final details have yet been worked out with reference to the vicinity of Vancouver. Plans are now being drawn up in connection with Vancouver island and the northern portions along Johnstone strait and off Prince Rupert.
Is there any special report in connection with fortifications around the city of Vancouver?
A special report has been prepared in connection with Vancouver, Victoria, Esquimalt and Prince Rupert.
Is anything being done in the defence program in connection with Queen Charlotte islands?

That
situation has been very carefully surveyed and reviewed in the last six months.

It seems to me that there are two kinds of works contemplated in this item; there are historic works and military works. I have no objection at all to the work that is to be done on the citadel at Quebec, which is a great historic monument, but I do not believe it is worth much from the military point of view, because a shell might destroy it. Those old walls which could resist the cannon balls of days gone by are not so impregnable now. I will not ask the minister to tell the committee where they are located, but I should like to know whether this includes some anti-aircraft defence?
This particular vote deals with emplacements in connection with coast defence, batteries or antiaircraft guns, et cetera. The guns themselves will be under another vote.
Can the minister tell me, roughly speaking, what will be the total in connection with so-called historic work, rebuilding or military construction?

The
amount is small, $30,000.
What amount is being spent on coastal defence in the east as compared with the Pacific?
I speak only from memory, but it is about $3,500,000 as against $7,000,000. It is about $11,000,000 altogether.
What amount is being spent for the improvement of the walls in the city of Quebec? Is the amount spent there considered a military work in the national defence scheme?

It is not in the slightest, but during recent years when the administration of unemployment in connection with the camps was to a certain extent under the Department of National Defence this work was carried out. In my opinion this

vote should not be under the Department of National Defence but under some other department. It has been cut down but we are trying to do the best we can.
What appropriation has been made for the defence of the prairie country through Churchill and Hudson bay?
That question also is being considered, but no specific developments have yet taken place.
Am I right in assuming that this amount now voted represents about fifty per cent of the program contemplated?

Yes, but in regard to one specific item only, that for $895,000, which deals with the preliminary steps that must be taken with reference to certain emplacements and defences in four or five places along the Pacific coast. The amount asked for this year-that is, only for work that can be done this year-is $895,000, and it is expected that a similar amount will be required at some future time.

Who prepares the plans? Is there in the department a council or a general staff on whom the minister relies for advice as to suitable plans and so forth? Will he inform the committee as to the personnel of any such council.

That
question was carefully considered by some of the officers from headquarters in Ottawa in consultation with officers in the various districts and also with an outside expert who gave their opinion with regard to Pacific coast defence.
Does that include officers on exchange from Great Britain?
One officer came out especially in connection with this work and was here about two months.
What points in eastern Canada does the minister propose to defend, and particularly what ports in the maritime provinces? What is the nature of the defence?

Speaking generally the reply would be that mostly in the vicinity of the leading ports of the maritime provinces these plans are under consideration. Of course the full development cannot take place with the amounts now asked for.
I noticed there was nothing in the estimates but engineering services for New Brunswick. I was wondering if they proposed any defences for the harbours.

That
question is being considered at the present
time, I have had correspondence on that, and when I have a reply I shall be glad to let my hon, friend have a copy.
Mr. MacNlEIL:	In view of the fact that
experts of the British war office have advised the department in regard to these fortifications, is it fair to assume that our coast defence plan is part of an empire defence plan, and that provision is being made for establishments in Canada as bases for imperial forces?

No, it is not. These services were asked for by the Department of National Defence, and before this officer arrived our own officers had worked out plans, and speaking broadly and generally the recommendations agreed in each case.
Did Major B. D. C. Treat have anything to do with it?

He is
the gentleman I have been speaking of for the last ten minutes.

I like so much to hear of him. But I do not see the use of having him here if he has only repeated what others have said. Probably he spoke only after having heard the good Canadians-I know there are some in the department-and then repeated that, and so he was a great man. Why does not the minister leave him outside of this country?-because he is of no use at all.
I understand the minister said the other day that an amount of $2,600,000 voted last year was not spent during the year.
No, that is not correct. It was voted last year for purposes which this year are not included in the estimates of the Department of National Defence.
That money was spent?

Yes,
much of it was.

To clarify the atmosphere
could the minister tell us from the point of view of experience and of science whether it is feasible for a belligerent to come from Europe to Canada with aeroplanes and attack the cities of this country?

I certainly do think it possible, not only with long range aircraft of modern types but also

Supply-Defence-Engineers
through the development of aircraft carriers. It is quite possible under modem conditions to have a raid on Canadian coasts and cities.

I should further like to
know this. I understand that if war is declared this country is concerned in seeing our trade continue, our goods shipped overseas and our avenues of trade kept open. Am I correct in saying that ships loaded with our goods could not go outside the three mile limit, otherwise we would become belligerents? If so, we must have warships to protect our merchant shipping, and after our shipping goes outside the three mile limit it must be protected by the British navy.

That of course raises the very difficult general question of neutrality in war time. Anyone will realize at once in view of Canada's very modest naval strength that it would be entirely impossible for us to protect our own trade routes. All we can hope to do is to protect the focal areas, that is, the points at which the trade routes from other countries converge upon our harbour mouths and shipping terminals on both coasts. Our defence against raiders or aircraft carriers must of necessity be limited, in view of the modest forces we have, to our own territorial waters.

I thank the minister for the information, which I think it is well that the people should have, especially those who oppose this estimate, so that they may know what the situation would be if war were declared.
War declared by whom, and between what nations?

By any European country or by any American country, in which European countries might become involved. I think it my duty to declare now the reason I am bound to vote for these estimates. It is, first, for the reasons which have been explained by the minister, and, second, because, having asked my constituents to tell me what to do,-because after all I am only their spokesman in the House of Commons-they held a general meeting and passed a resolution by a large majority in favour of this government spending that amount of money for national defence. The resolution has two other paragraphs, in one of which they state that in case of war they want this parliament to ask the people through a referendum whether they are willing to take part in any European war. And if there is such a referendum they ask that nobody be permitted to vote except those residing in Canada. But for the time being I am perfectly free and I am in duty bound to vote for these estimates.
I assume this program has been prepared under the advice of the minister's military experts. May I ask if they were Canadian officers or imperial officers?

They
were all Canadian officers except the one to whom I referred. An officer was asked for by the department, to come from England especially to advise on coast defences. He was here about two months and he acted in cooperation with our own officers of all three services.
And he had information on this very subject, which was technical information that the government desired.
Exactly. He is supposed to be, and I believe is, one of the leading specialists on fortification works.

If the danger from aircraft is a determining factor we should examine more closely the minister's statement. He gave it as his opinion that we are in danger from air raids. There are two ways in which such raids could be made, as he suggested. One is by a return flight of aircraft from Europe, which I think it can be stated generally is at present a practical impossibility. A ship would have to refuel on this side. Where would it refuel?

It might go to the hon.
member's house.

It would not find gasoline in my house with which to refuel. The second way would be by aircraft carrier. In the event of war and aircraft carriers being used, if we are to prevent air raids we shall have to prevent the coming of the carrier. How could two destroyers possibly cope with that situation? We have to bear in mind that in any war we should be involved largely on account of our association with some other country. It might be because of proximity to the United States, or because of our connection with Great Britain, even if we declared neutrality. We must remember that either of those nations has a navy powerful enough to prevent the passage of aircraft carriers across the Atlantic, and would be prepared to stop them for their own protection and the protection of their trade routes. I believe the endeavour to frighten people with the thought that we are defending ourselves against air raids is making the house rather ridiculous, especially when we examine the matter in the light of cold reason. We are not in danger of air raids, and I was greatly amused to read that

following the discussion in the house last week an official in the department suggested that a special department should be installed in McGill university to teach people how to look after themselves in the event of air raids. That sort of thing, it seems to me, is an attempt to play upon the nerves of people who have not thought the matter out. I suggest that we examine the minister's statement in the light of actual physical possibilities.

The vote of $2,816,950 for engineer services and works must be considered without fear or favour. So long as the king of the United Kingdom is the king of Canada, and so long as we are linked with Great Britain and are a part of the British Empire I shall have no objection to a reasonable expenditure in the defence of Canada. As Canada is part of the British Empire, in looking to our defence we are to a certain extent defending the British Empire. That is my humble view, and the opinion I have reached after having visited my home and having discussed the matter with sound-thinking Canadians who hold a similar view. They are interested in the defence of Canada from coast to coast, but they do not want to go further than that. I shall not object to voting for the defence of Canada, so long as my mind is satisfied.
In this instance I am asked to vote $2,816,950, representing a two-thirds increase. We must consider, first of all, that except in the event of civil war any attack must come from the outside. In that event would it come from Europe or from Asia? We do not know. It may or it may not come; I am not ready to discuss that point. It would take a technician, possibly an officer of the army, a man of great experience or a university professor to discuss it. In my view, however, if a thing is done it must be well done. I do not say that money should be wasted, and in this connection I would apply the same reasoning as I do in connection with the dragoons. Their work was not well done, and it might better have been dispensed with. I hope in future the guard will have better horses, or will not parade before the parliament buildings.
Defence must be appropriate. This is not a matter of voting money for the relief of unemployed; it is not something to be done by the Department of Labour or the Department of Public Works. This is a vote for the defence of Canada, and a serious matter. I have no objection to defence, provided we have reasonable grounds for believing that an attack can be made and that the amount 31111-70
voted will provide improved works, and a defence sufficient to prevent an enemy from entering the country.
There is something else which strikes me, but which I have not yet expressed. I make this observation as a Liberal, and following the principles laid down at the St. Roch hotel by my Quebec leader, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I wonder whether this is not part of the H.I.P.-the home improvement plan-with Mr. Purvis at its head. I find it a great mistake to have him in charge of the unemployment business. He is the man who controls the manufacture of explosives, and also eelanese and cellophane. I wonder whether he is not the nigger in the wood pile in that business. He may have done much more than B. D. C. Treat from Surrey, England. I should like to have this point clear. Notice that the man in charge of unemployment relief in Canada, the head of the employment commission, is our own little Zaharoff-a most incredible thing-our pocket edition of Zaharoff. He is head of the employment commission. I ask the minister honestly to tell the committee if Purvis had anything to do, directly or indirectly, with the increase in the votes for the Department of National Defence?
I have pleasure in informing the hon. member that I never had the privilege of discussing any items in the defence estimates with Mr. A. B. Purvis.
So much the better.
Are the expenditures inr-volved in this item for the purpose of defending Canada against exterior aggression?

It is all
for purposes within Canada, and for no other purpose.
But could the minister make a distinction, and state whether the expenditures are to protect Canada from exterior aggression?
Certainly, they are all for that.

I ask that because I recall the words of the Prime Minister. After reviewing our friendy relations with other countries, recalling our geographical position and drawing a picture of the international situation he said, as reported at page 1048 of Hansard:
On the whole there has been some improvement, a less tense strain in the international situation.

He described Canada as the most secure of all countries, and then said, as reported at page 1050:
It is not contended that danger is great for us. There is a danger but so far as Canada is concerned it is, as I have already pointed out, an incidental contingency. Relatively our danger is small.
I said before, and I now repeat that I am ready to vote every dollar which I believe necessary for the protection of Canada, but for the protection of Canada alone. Although I have full confidence in the words of the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence, I cannot convince myself that so large an increase is necessary for the protection of Canada, and Canada alone. I may be wrong in my fear; I hope I am. I would rather be wrong than have others wrong. Although I would be willing to support the item, I am reluctant to support so large an increase, particularly in this year when we need every dollar to run the country. I do not know what deficit will be shown when the budget is brought down on Thursday. We may foresee, however, that it will be large, and that we may have a further deficit next year. I believe the Prime Minister said that the defence force had been neglected during the last few years, for reasons of economy, and that this program was not presented last year on account of the European situation due to the Italian war with Ethiopia. But economies are just as necessary to-day as they were during the last five years and unless it is absolutely necessary, I do not think there should be any increase in the military estimates.

I think this increase is merely the thin end of the wedge; it is just an illustration of what future governments will be asking for. The present government is asking for approximately $1,000,000 to carry on the defence of a small part of our Pacific coast line. The minister has informed the committee that next year a similar amount will be required in order to complete the defences of one portion of the Pacific coast. If approximately $2,000,000 is required to provide this limited defence, no one knows what amounts we may be asked for in future years in order to provide a complete defence of both our Atlantic and Pacific coasts. I am not a military expert, but speaking as a layman I contend that it is impossible for any Canadian government completely to defend our Atlantic and Pacific coasts with the resources at their disposal. In making this statement I am taking into account that our air defences may also 'be considered as part of our coastal defences. In a matter of this kind the minister is entitled to have the best expert advice available, and I ask him if it is his opinion
/"Mr. Paymond.]
or the opinion of his expert advisers that this $2,000,000 will provide adequate defences for that part of the country to meet any contingency the government might have in mind.

I do not prebend to be an expert on these matters, but the beet advice which I have received as minister of the department from those competent to give advice is that these amounts will afford reasonable protection.
What does the minister mean when he says, " will afford reasonable protection "?

The
money being voted this year and what will be necessary next year.
Therefore, unless something unexpected develops, these amounts will be sufficient to take care of the defences of the country so far as the minister's department is concerned?
I would not commit myself as to any development in the future.

In discussing the coastal defence plan for the Pacific coast- the minister stated in the neighbourhood of Esquimau there would be some concentration of defence in the nature of gun emplacements and various kinds of fortifications. I do not think we should overlook the fact that Esquimalt is a British naval base. Is it fair to assume that the British naval authorities will place British naval guns in these emplacements in order to repel capital ships? It is difficult for me to believe that the Department of National Defence will be in a position to place at that point guns sufficiently powerful to repel raiders of any first class power, considering the range and calibre- of the guns usually found on the capital ships of the grea-t powers. In concentrating our defences at Esquimalt -are we not asking for trouble? Are we not -adopting a provocative measure of defence? Will we not be involved in any conflict in which the British Empire may be involved?

Esquimalt is a Canadian base and is Canadian controlled. There is no suggestion whatsoever, so far as my knowledge goes, that the British government will place any guns for the defence of Esquimalt. We have -had some 9.2 guns at -this point for some years. These guns were ordered relined and remounted last year -and it is intended to supplement the number of guns during the present year.

Is not Esquimalt the base for the Pacific squadron of -the British fleet?

At one time it was a regular base but it is no longer. It is used now only for stores and coaling purposes.

Is there any arrangement between the Canadian and British governments whereby a British warship may come into that port at any hour and for any purpose? Is there any understanding 'that in the event of hostilities Esquimau will be defended by the British navy?
I do not think the latter observation is quite justifiable. For years naval stores have been kept at Halifax and Esquimalt, to 'be used when desired.

The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) has made a point which we should remember. He stated that unless our coasts are adequately defended, any defences will be simply provocative. We must either go the whole hog or remain in such a position as not to be a menace to any other nation. The minister says that he does not anticipate large expenditures in future years. A short time ago I asked the minister if it was contemplated to defend Churchill, and he told me not this year. If we are going to defend our coast lines adequately, these key points will all have to be defended. If we once put our feet along this path of providing gun emplacements. coastal defences and so on, we must realize that we may be led much farther than we are given to understand today we will be. I am thoroughly convinced of that, and that is one reason why I am opposing this estimate. I believe that with a coast line such as we have, to do as the government intends will mean embarking upon a course which will be more or less provocative and interfere with any neutrality we may desire to observe in the future.
Is it the intention of the Minister of National Defence to ask for increased estimates for national defence year after year?

As I said before, I cannot state at the present moment what the estimates for next year will be. They will be governed by conditions prevailing at that time. However, I can tell my hon. friend that at the present time there is no plan to provide for increased estimates. This matter will be decided by the government in the light of conditions existing at that time.

Are our coastal defences designed to repel naval vessels and aircraft?
31111-70}
To repel one or the other or both.

So far I have not made
any declaration on this important matter and before doing so I wanted to hear what explanations the minister had to make. I have just one or two remarks to make before 1 declare definitely my intention to vote for this amendment. Whether or not we like it,, we must face the state of affairs which exists-at the present time. I am not at all satisfied with the explanations which have been given for this large increase.
_ The other day mention was made about internal protection; the communists were after us; we were all to be smashed between Calgary, Fort William and Montreal. But to-day it is all different. It is aeroplanes now. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that the protection which we are providing against the danger is ridiculous. Next it is the protection of air ports. I agree with the statement which has been made that the money to be spent in that regard will be a mere drop in the bucket. The hon., member for Ghambly-Rouville (Mr. Dupuis), in putting a question a moment ago, said, "If war is declared." I asked him by whom and between whom, and he did not reply. The reply we had received a few minutes before from the Minister of National Defence was that we must prepare for the future. He did not know what would be done next year. "Conditions prevailing throughout the world," he said, "would have to guide us." Now is it not remarkable, Mr. Chairman, that at the very moment when we are jumping into an increased military expenditure of a couple of millions, the other side decides not to spend anything on colonial protection. As the hon. member for Beau-harnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) said the other day, it is a mere coincidence, but a coincidence which should open our eyes.
We are gradually getting into war, and we may as well face the issue. For my part, that is what I say. I say it is a question not of local defence, but a war defence. I am against war; I am going to take my stand against it right now. I have not forgotten what took place from 1914 to 1918. There were heroes, there were great soldiers, there were friends of mine who went to the front and wrote their names in history. I had two brothers there, one of whom was wounded, who spent three and a half years at the front and fought with courage. But during the last twenty years we have been in the grip of an agony as a result of the war, and we wasted money the repayment of which will be a 'burden for generations to come. We go into our cities

The women ^nd children want fair protection, and here [DOT]this government comes with an increase of two million dollars for armaments. The province of Quebec is in the confederation and m the British Empire, and we are ready I speak for my riding-to shoulder our proper responsibility, 'but this is not a request that should come at this time, and for my part I am going to vote for the amendment.

Will the minister explain vhat the air-conditioning item for Ottawa s for.

Would the minister give

This item is largely for construction work. Would it not be possible to give a great deal of that work to the unemployed veterans? I understand that about

I wanted to ask the
minister to amplify the remarks he made in his speech last week with regard to the investigation he has been carrying on to find out what industrial units could be utilized for the supply of equipment and munitions and so on.
That matter comes under the general stores vote. I shall be glad to deal with it at that time.
For what sizes of guns are the emplacements being built on the west coast?

The guns that are now there, but were outmoded, were 9-2 guns, but they are being reconditioned, relined and remounted and will be as good as new when that work is completed. It was commenced last year. It is intended to supplement them with some six-inch guns and also, I believe, with some others.
Is much to be spent by way of expropriation of properties?
I could not give a definite answer. I should not think the amount would be very large. So far as possible we are proceeding by expropriation or negotiation-preferably by expropriation.
Is there much property to be bought out of the amount that is to be voted at the present time?

I should think the amount will include the purchase of properties, but I do not suppose it will be very extensive, because in any case it is hoped these properties will not be located in congested areas.

One matter causes me
concern. In going over the reports of the Department of National Defence I find that amounts ranging from around $300,000 to approximately $1,000,000 have been voted each
year in succession for this particular purpose, engineer services and works, and I assume that the same men who are now planning our coastal defences have been aware of the dangers with which, it is alleged, we are threaten,ed at the present time. How does the minister account for the fact that notwithstanding these expenditures extending over a. long period of years he now states plainly that no coastal defence exists? Why was no provision made, when the department was first made aware of war preparations in Europe and on the Pacific, for the defence which is now being planned?

Of course my bon. friend will realize that I cannot answer for any of my predecessors. I can tell him that within one week of coming into office I took action to ascertain the present condition of these matters.

Another question: Could the minister roughly segregate the amount of this vote that is being spent on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts and the amount that is being devoted for purposes inland? To what extent is money being expended on the further construction of armouries and training grounds?
There is not a single cent for armouries, except a small amount for reconditioning. Not a cent is included in these estimates for new armouries.

I assume that the minister is planning adequate protection against aircraft. Is the department taking into consideration the danger of air raids from over the arctic circle-which may not be as incredible as at the moment it may sound? In all seriousness, it has been shown by aviation experts in recent years that the shortest route to this country from some of those countries which we are led to believe may now be threatening Canada is over the arctic circle into the very centre of Canada. Is the defence plan taking into consideration protection against aircraft raids from that directiop?
Provision in that respect is being considered and, I believe, a report on the matter will be made to the department.

Where will these stores, particularly guns and munitions, be purchased?
As far as possible we are endeavouring to have them purchased in Canada.
To what extent will that be done?

We have a committee now surveying all resources, both public and private, in the Dominion of Canada, with that purpose in view. We have not yet reached the stage of production of ammunition to any extent in the dominion, but the decided objective is, on account of the difficulty of obtaining these supplies outside the country, to have them manufactured in Canada.
Is it intended to encourage the production of these stores in Canada and to set up factories for that purpose?

Of course it would take some time to establish public factories for that purpose. At the present time, for the immediate emergency, it has been decided to cooperate with private industry, exercising proper supervision and control.

Are General Motors making or proposing to make munitions or equipment for the department? Let me explain what I have in mind. There has been a rumour, for example, that the assembly plant at Regina is to be converted into a munitions factory by the General Motors corporation. I have read that in western papers.

I have no information in that regard, and I do not believe that is the case. The only work which that corporation is doing for the department is trying to develop a tractor; as I recall, the sum of $4,500 has been expended in that work.

Of course many of our industrial plants could be readily converted into munitions factories, and I believe that a good deal of the urge for rearmament is coming from industrialists who see the prospect

of profit. That is the reason I should like to see something done to curtail possible munitions profits. One other question. I notice that in this item is included ammunition and guns and supplies. Following the question of the hon. member for Selkirk, may I ask, are we buying munitions from abroad? To be more specific, are we experimenting with any guns produced in Czechoslovakia? I have in mind the Bren machine gun. If so, what are we paying for these guns?

I believe it was the year before last that two were ordered by the department; ten more are now on order. The Bren is a new automatic machine gun which up to now has been manufactured in Czechoslovakia. I understand that the rights of the manufacturer have been purchased by the British government and that they are to construct as soon as possible a factory in the United Kingdom for the extensive production of that type of gun. The department has been looking into the question with a view to having the gun manufactured in Canada.
What are we paying for these guns?
I believe we paid $1,000 apiece for the first two.

Anyone who has seen one of these guns and compared it with an automobile realizes that there is very little mechanism about it. These guns are manufactured, particularly under mass production, very cheaply, and here we are paying $1,000 apiece for machine guns from Czechoslovakia, probably from a factory owned by a gang of international munition makers, possibly to practise slaughter upon other nations who are using exactly the same gun to slaughter Canadian boys. It seems to me that if we are going to buy guns we ought to buy them without encouraging these enormous profits that are being made by the munition companies, and I call attention particularly to this gun from Czechoslovakia. We are paying $1,000 each for these guns and I venture to say they can be made for at least a quarter the cost of a Ford car.

I have nothing to add to what I said the other day by way of protest against this program of increased armaments. I accept without hesitation, of course, the statement made by the Prime Minister that we have not made any commitments, but it is not always within the power of one individual to decide what the future will bring, and I am afraid that this policy now initiated with the best of motives will

lead us in the wrong direction. I am opposed to it for the reasons I stated the other day, and therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lacroix), that item 63 of the estimates of the Department of National Defence be reduced by $3,509,499.
