speechtext: I may point out that an amendment such as this does not require a seconder.

The other day the Minister of National Defence, speaking on the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), said:
We have reduced the military establishment of this country from 135,000 to 90,000; in fact we have done that within1 twelve months. All we are doing now is to see to it that this small force shall be properly equipped.
I understand that the item now under discussion is to provide for some equipment.
That is correct.
I am surprised that there is an increase. If the military establishment has been reduced from 135,000 to 90,000, the cost of equipment should be reduced. Will the minister be kind enough to explain?

There was no equipment to speak of before. We have reduced the paper strength, as it is called, of the militia forces from 135,000 to a total of about 90,000. The actual training strength will not be very much changed, but under the old form there was very little equipment available. What equipment we had was largely obsolete, and we are now endeavouring to get some modern guns and machine guns, and other things necessary for an effective and efficient militia force in the dominion. This is to replace equipment that has become obsolete and worn out and to obtain more adequate equipment for our forces.
How was the money voted last year under a similar item spent?
It was spent for the same purpose, but it was not nearly sufficient to proceed with the mechanization of the reorganized forces of Canada.
Is this just for the present year?
It was preliminary to what we are doing now.

The minister must realize that both in this house and outside there is a strong volume of opinion against this vast increase. It is coming to be realized more and
more even in this chamber, as we have seen this afternoon, that the vast amount of money we are asked to spend on these items will not make Canada any more secure against attack than it was last year and that these increased expenditures on armaments will not secure our neutrality to any greater extent. A certain number of people who stand to gain by these expenditures will be heartily in favour of this vast increase. The armament manufacturers or those who intend to manufacture armaments and those who have to deal with war materials will all be glad to see this increase, and in my opinion the increase this year is merely the prelude to greater increases to be asked for in this chamber in future years. I believe this is merely the thin end of the wedge, and the minister has more or less admitted it. It is my experience that those who run departments are always anxious to have the most efficient and the greatest department anywhere. In municipal affairs I have found the same thing. The head of the fire department wants the greatest fire-fighting apparatus to be found anywhere in the world, and the same applies to the war department. Now we are setting up a war department we are entering upon a vast expenditure for armaments.
I wish to refer to a statement made by the minister with regard to the purchase of munitions. I think it would be better if he did not go outside to purchase munitions. If the government is going to go into the purchase of armaments, in my opinion it should, as far as possible, establish its own munition plants. I do not think the minister has far to go at the present time. There is no need at this stage, for him to go to private armament manufacturers and ask them to put in bids, for in the last war the railway shops of Canada were able to turn out munitions, and I was told that they did so as efficiently and as cheaply as the private manufacturers could produce them, if not more so. If such is the case I want to take the profits out of this whole manufacture of munitions, if we can do it by the government owning, controlling and operating the munition factories. Then perhaps the pressure from outside by those who produce these goods would not be as strong as it is now. I should like to know whether the minister has canvassed the situation recently to see whether the government itself could not undertake the manufacture of munitions in plants in which they were manufactured during the last year. I have reference to the railway shops.

I find
myself in agreement with much of what the hon. member has said, and the government took action some time ago along the lines he
Supply-D efe nee-Stores

now suggests. An interdepartmental committee was appointed some months ago to make an industrial survey of the whole of Canada. That committee has been functioning. There is also in the Department of National Defence under the master general of the ordnance a joint army, navy and air supply committee, and that committee has already surveyed about sixty or seventy industrial plants throughout the dominion. It has also been instructed to survey the public plants of the kind to which my hon. friend has referred with a view to making an up to date report as to how far, in the event of an emergency, these plants could be used for public purposes. So that what my hon. friend advocates has been carried out for the last several months.

The minister says that in case of emergency these plants will be utilized. But I am not now referring to a case of emergency, unless he calls present conditions a case of emergency. I am referring to the money which we are asked to vote in this item, which is to go for the purchase of munitions. I want to know whether the minister can give an undertaking that the supplies for which this money is now being voted could not be manufactured in the railway shops, in plants which are partly or wholly under government control and ownership. A survey may have been made, but I want to know whether there is going to be a start made and these shops owned by the government and people of Canada kept in operation, because from these shops I am sure he will get just as good an article as, if not better than, that produced under private ownership.

A considerable amount under this vote we are considering will go to the government-owned institutions at Valcartier and the dominion arsenal at Quebec. In addition we are surveying the plants to which the hon. member has referred to see how far they can be used for the purpose.
Are there government-owned plants outside the railway shops capable of manufacturing munitions?
Yes.
Where are they?
There are factories in Canada which did produce munitions during the war and would be willing to do so again if given the opportunity.
But those are privately-owned institutions?
Yes.

But what I want is to get the manufacture of these munitions entirely out of private hands. What I am asking is a complete survey of government-owned institutions capable of manufacturing munitions required by the government. If the minister could have that survey made, it would meet with the approval of people inside and outside this house.
That is being done at the present time, in regard to both publicly and privately-owned plants.

Let me say to the hon. member who has just spoken and to hon. gentlemen opposite who supported the motion of want of confidence in the government, that they cannot blow hot and cold. They must either stand b}' their guns or desert their guns. Having found that a vast majority of this house and a tremendous body of public opinion in this country are favourable to the policy of the government as brought down by the Minister of National Defence, he asks the minister, in whom he votedi want of confidence, whether he will give an undertaking. I ask him what good that undertaking would be to him after having voted no confidence in the minister.
Then the hon, member referred to defences on the Atlantic and the Pacific and asked what good were they. I did not speak on the amendment, but let me remind him that the country to the south of us is the United States. There is to-day what is called an imaginary boundary line between this country and that, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific. If the hon. member goes out in front of this building he will see carved deep in the stone over the main entrance these words: The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
Is it the responsibility of the government, is it the responsibility of this house, is it the responsibility of this country to defend these gates? If we do not defend them, then we are vulnerable to any enemy which may attack the United States, and then what happens? The enemy will enter Canada through these gates, and not only shall we be at once in the position of becoming belligerents, but the Americans will have to defend themselves against enemies invading their country through ours. Therefore the American government will have to fortify that imaginary boundary line from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Let my hon. friends opposite who voted want of confidence in the government on this most important and vital matter answer that question as to whether they are in favour of

Supply-Defence-Stores
reasonable defence of the gates of this country both east and west and the great St. Lawrence river, or whether they are in favour of a do-nothing policy, and simply telling the government which is in power to-day, You are no good for the fricassee; you are no good for the soup, and like the rabbit that ran away, you are no good at all. That, Mr. Chairman, is the position of my hon. friends led by the hon. gentleman in the front seat who is laughing on the front of his face. But the people of this country understand the situation, as does this house.

Mr. Chairman, my object in rising is to point out to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) that in connection with securing a supply of arms and munitions sufficient to meet the requirements of the dominion, serious consideration should be given to using the facilities available in the constituency of Victoria, Ontario, which I have the honour to represent. With respect to overseas orders for arms and munitions which are coming to Canada, I do not believe the government would be justified in interfering with the private corporations which are filling these orders for arms and munitions. Yet, in connection with the supply of these materials for use, if needed, in our own country, the question is entirely different, and I believe it would be a sound policy for the government to manufacture arms and munitions for our own defence, when required. This policy would prevent private corporations from making exorbitant profits, as happened during the great war.
If present government facilities are operating at full capacity, and are not adequate, then we should carefully supervise any additional contracts for war material. I referred in my opening remarks to the dominion arsenal number two located at Lindsay, Ontario. This is a plant covering several acres, the buildings of which are in a reasonable state of repair. It is true some additional material and machinery of the newer type would have to be acquired. Yet the amount of money necessary to place the plant in perfect running order would not be an unreasonable sum. It should not be forgotten that in order to provide sidewalks, roads and other necessary civic services for the arsenal, the town of Lindsay spent from $75,000 to $100,000, a large amount of money for a town of only eight thousand people. This
has added materially to the burdens of the corporation, which at the present time is receiving very little in reit-urn. The plant is the property of the dominion government. The item under discussion contains a substantial expenditure for arms and munitions, and I desire that the department supervised by the Minister of National Defence give consideration to reopening this plant in the present emergency, and that the manufacture of these materials be carried on at this plant under the direct supervision of the Department of National Defence.

I do not agree with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) said just before six o'clock. There are in Canada firms equipped to make the various items required, and they have no connection whatsoever with international munitions makers. One firm I have in mind is John Bertram and Sons Company, Limited, of Dundas, Ontario. That firm is one hundred per cent Canadian, employs Canadian workmen and is fully equipped to manufacture either big guns or munitions.

Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario (Mr. McNevin), may I say I had the pleasure of visiting Lindsay during the last year, and accompanied by officials of the department made a thorough inspection of the buildings and properties there. The government of Canada has in the properties at Lindsay a very considerable investment, amounting to about $800,000 for the land and $800,000 for the buildings, or a total of $1,700,000. I can assure the hon. member that this year the department will make a careful survey of the possibility of utilizing the property now in possession of the government, in connection with projects being developed.
May I tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), that there is no suggestion of any pressure in regard to any government policy, so far as firms in Canada are concerned. This is entirely regardless of any pressure or suggestions by any firms of any kind in Canada.
I wish to thank the minister for his explanation. I am satisfied the government will give consideration to the matter.

May I say a word or two in comment on what the minister has said in reference to the Lindsay arsenal. I know he was there, because I made a thorough inspection of the plant myself. In my view Lindsay is particularly well situated. I am
Supply-Defence-Stores

familiar with the town and the surrounding country, and I believe it is well situated for the work the minister had in mind.
When he was speaking before the dinner recess the minister said that the department intended to do similar work at Yalcartier and, if I remember correctly, at Montreal-
At Quebec.

Yes. At that time I noticed he did not mention Lindsay. I had intended to bring the fact to his attention, because of all places mentioned I believe Lindsay has the best location. Valcartier could be blown off the map by aeroplane invasion, but it would take an aeroplane different from what we have to-day to cross the sea and then go as far west as Lindsay. Besides, the topography of the land about Lindsay lends protection, and its waterways offer points of landing for seaplanes. The buildings are as the minister described them.
May I now say a word on behalf of the minister's staff, at the Lindsay arsenal, because they all strike me as being competent men. I saw that they had covered all the equipment with grease, which is a first class protection, and I believe a word of commendation now and then from the head of the department would mean a great deal to men who take care sufficient to protect the valuable equipment in the plant. My understanding is that the machines could be put into instant operation. During the great war large quantities of munitions were made there, and ample testing places are available. I should like to encourage the minister to go the whole way in providing work for Lindsay workmen along with those of Yalcartier and Quebec. Lindsay is so far removed from possible attack that anything done by the department at that point would be safe from attack by sea.

In connection with the survey made of the plant at Lindsay, may I say to the hon. member that to put the plant into shape for production of small arms and ammunition would cost in the neighbourhood of $400,000. To equip the plant with the necessary new machines to produce small arms and munitions would cost perhaps a million dollars.

The minister seems to be of opinion that we may be subject to air attack. I shall not argue the point with him, but shall ask him this question: In the defence estimates what provision is being made to secure supplies to reassure the civilian

population that sufficient preparations will be ready to keep communities safe from air attack?

The only answer I can make is that by the cooperation of the three branches of the service we hope to be in a position to meet any such aggression, if it comes. I did not get the drift of the hon. member's question, and I do not know if he was referring to food supplies.

No, I am referring to actual defence from air attack. I think it is generally realized that an air raid would consist largely in the dropping of bombs. There are three types of bombs, namely the explosive bomb, the gas bomb and the incendiary bomb. Of the three I believe the last is by far the worst. It is all very well to say that the three branches of our military defence will cooperate to ward off attack, but I would direct attention to the fact that the Prime Minister of Great Britain told the British House of Commons that aeroplanes were not meant for defensive purposes and that it would be impossible through the use of planes to defend a city from aerial attack. If these are defence estimates, what defence are we providing for the people of Canada? Are we going to rely upon a few guns stuck here and there? I contend that that is no defence whatsoever. If the minister is right, our real defence lies in our preparedness to meet conditions which will arise should an air attack occur. I believe the purpose of such an attack would be to strike panic into the hearts of the people so that they would compel whatever government may be in power at the time to sue for peace. This brings me back to the point I made this afternoon, that armaments such as wTe can provide are simply provocative and would in my opinion invite a potential enemy to strike terror into the hearts of our people. What defence is the department providing in the event of air raids?

As I said before, I do not pretend to be a superstrategist like my hon. friend, but I do suggest that aeroplanes provide the best defence against air raids. The only defence my hon. friends are willing to provide is no defence at all; they are ready to leave Canada entirely defenceless. We are making a reasonable effort to meet any possible aggression and 1 think we are all united in the hope that there will never be any need for these defences. We intend to provide on our coasts a few high speed aeroplanes which will work in cooperation wdth the other services.

Supply-Defence-Stores

That does not answer
my question. I want to know what preparations the department is making to protect our people from incendiary and gas bombs. I realize it would be almost impossible to provide protection against explosive bombs. As we all know from our general reading, the defence program of Great Britain has been concentrated upon this particular problem.
The best methods which the combined skill of the technical advisers of the department can devise will be taken and these will be used in conjunction with the precautionary measures already taken.
For the convenience and education of the hon. gentleman, perhaps the minister could have all the plans of strategy published in the Canada Gazette.

As the minister is well
aware, it does not require a superstrategist to answer the question asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). In the event of an air raid the civilian population will suffer. The minister is well aware that military strategists of the first rank agree that the only defence against air attack is retaliation and we would have no opportunity to engage in such retaliation. I think special provision should be made to protect the women and children in the principal harbours on both our coasts. The minister should consider the building of bomb proof and gas proof shelters in order that the civilian population will not suffer. Is this defence merely for the small number of troops who will be actually manning the guns at these points? This matter is being considered in other countries and I cannot understand why the minister brushes our suggestions aside with derision, particularly as they concern the women and children of this dominion.

I may
say that every single cent of these estimates might possibly be used for the protection of the women and children of Canada. I do not think my hon. friend is very helpful when he suggests that there should be no protection whatsoever.

My question still remains
unanswered. Is any provision being made for the construction of shelters in the event of air raids?

It does not require a
military strategist to realize that should any country attack Canada by air, it would first of all establish an aeroplane base somewhere
in Canada. If we did not have planes available to attack that base, we would be powerless.

Does this item include anything for the purchase of ordnance, or is it just for the purchase of rifles and cartridges?

As I
said before, there is in this vote an item amounting to $3,795,331 for artillery stores, or an increase of $2,858,616.
About one-third of this vote will1 be used for the purchase of ordnance?

More
than one-third for artillery stores.
Will this item cover the purchase of anti-aircraft guns?
There are two sections of anti-aircraft artillery, including munitions for mobile units and excluding coast defence but available for these purposes which would cost about $350,000.
Items 62, 63, 64 and 65 are closely connected. One covers the building of fortifications and the providing of bases for guns. If I am not mistaken, that would be under item 62?

Quite
right.	.

Then the guns and
ammunition would come under item 63, general stores. These things would be used by the non-permanent and permanent militia, covered by items 64 and 65. I voted for the reduction of item 62 for several reasons, one of which was the fact that it covered the maintenance of historical buildings which I felt should be placed under the control of our parks commission. This shows that there is little order in the departments of government Will the minister tell me if the final say in the purchase of the items covered under general stores will be left to him or will that be decided by a commission? I should like to know also if item 63 is under his control?

Yes,
under the control of the governor in council.
Supply-Defence-Stores

Thank you. This is how I understand government, Mr. Chairman, that every minister shall be boss of his own department, and shall not be bothered by commissions around him on which he can lean to escape responsibility. There is one thing that struck me in the minister's explanation a few moments ago with regard to Mr. Purvis. I am very much concerned about this item for general stores; I was very much afraid, and I think I still have reason to believe, that Mr. Purvis might be the nigger in the wood pile, but I will take the word of the minister that he has never spoken to Mr. Purvis about the increase in the military vote. I think that is a fair interpretation of the minister's words. I do not need to tell the committee that soldiers cannot fight with wooden guns or air rifles,, like children. They must have real guns, and real ammunition for them, I admit. If the first item had been reduced, I would have voted for a proportional reduction in item 63, because as there would have been less engineering services and less work, the material required should also have been less.
But I will go the limit. I will take the word of the minister this time, but I promise that I shall scrutinize the other items very closely. Undoubtedly if we are to have a permanent and a non-permanent force, our soldiers should be reasonably well equipped; otherwise let us dispense entirely with the Department of National Defence. If we have soldiers, they must have clothes, be protected- against the cold in winter and be well cared for while they serve in the army; otherwise let us reduce the whole vote for this department to one dollar or one cent. But if we are to have an army, we must look after our soldiers in peace time as well as in war. That is my humble view, and therefore I shall vote against the amendment to this item. I do not know what I shall do on the others.
What is meant by mechanical water transport?

The
operation and maintenance of mechanical transport vehicles with the Royal Canadian Army Service Corps. The increase this year is $416, the amount being $25,401 this year as compared with $24,985 last year; other vehicles, last year $12,845, and this year $16,935, or an increase of $4,090. In the item for the purchase of motor transport vehicles there is a decrease from $33,263 last year to $28,757 this year. The amount for operation and maintenance of Royal Canadian Army Service Corps water transports is $7,450.

The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) before the dinner recess tried to make it appear that our attitude over here was not consistent with the attitude we took the other day. I maintain that it is absolutely consistent, and that in fact we are taking very much the same attitude as the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) took just a few moments ago. He said that if we were going to have soldiers we could not arm them with wooden guns. All things are relative, and it is just as logical to arm soldiers with wooden guns as to try to protect this dominion by expending the appropriations that are now before the committee. It is as impossible to do the one as the other. Our geography and our long coast line make it impossible for us to defend ourselves by making these expenditures.
Referring to the question we were discussing a moment ago as to the manufacture of munitions by the government or by private enterprise, I understand the minister stated that surveys had been made. I should like to ask how much of the supplies at present being used by the government was manufactured by government works, how much was supplied by private industry within the dominion, and what proportion we imported from other countries?
Is my hon. friend speaking of munitions only, or of all supplies?
Of all supplies.
Until the present year quite a lot of the supplies required by the department, ordinary supplies which any department might require, like clothing-
Leave out clothing.

So far as the supply of munitions is concerned we have been limited in recent years to the production of the Quebec arsenal, but now we have just about completed the filling group at Val-cartier, which is a dominion-owned institution operated in conjunction with the ammunition group at the arsenal in Quebec. We have had to import some munitions from other sources. It is hoped now, especially in view of the delay there would be in obtaining supplies from overseas, that most of our supplies can be manufactured in Canada. That is why the survey is now being made in regard to publicly-owned and private plants, the supervision of private manufactures or the utilization of available government-owned institutions.

Supply-Defence-Stores

That point is a very important one. If we have to have armaments and munitions of war for offence or defence, so far as possible they should be manufactured by the federal government rather than by private firms engaged in the manufacture of arms. To turn the work over to private enterprise would mean that we would be continually subjected to pressure to buy supplies. There are rumours floating around at the present time that are disquieting, and we should be very careful that we do not give occasion for such rumours to arise, or put ourselves into the position where we shall be subject to pressure in the future.
Did I understand from the minister that the survey is now almost completed?
It will take at least another year.

Assuming that it does take another year, there must be in the possession of the government at the present time quite a number of facts pertaining to sites now under government control and as to facilities which the government could command in the immediate future. Could sufficient arms and munitions be supplied in the government's own factories to meet present needs?

There
are two principles involved. The first would be to decide the question of complete public ownership of these utilities; the second, their capacity to produce sufficient quantities to meet requirements. My hon. friend will realize that it takes some time to instal new machinery-new jigs and dies and all the necessary implements of production-in any factory, publicly or privately owned. At the present time it seems essential to expedite as much as possible the production of these necessary supplies. There may be an immediate policy and a long range policy. A long range policy would doubtless, as it did in England, combine government-owned arsenals and institutions with the cooperation, attended by strict supervision, of private industries.

Has the minister at hand the contracts that were placed outside Canada for light and heavy artillery, small arms and tanks, et cetera, the countries in which they were placed, and the firms with which they were placed?
I do not think that in recent months we have placed any contracts of the kind my hon. friend has mentioned.
Do I fake it that no contracts were placed outside Canada?

There
were for aeroplanes, but that was twenty-four months ago.
None for small arms or artillery or 'tanks?
No, not recently.
Ls it proposed, in connection with the amount we are voting in the present estimates, that these arms and munitions be manufactured in publicly-owned plants here in Canada?

The hon. member will find very greatly increased amounts for production of these articles in arsenals which are now government-owned in the Dominion of Canada. It is a question whether these will be sufficient to meet the increased amount provided for in these estimates, and therefore it may be necessary, during this year at any rate, to cooperate with private industry, with, as I said before, the most rigid supervision. After all, with regard ito profits there are three elements: in the first place, supplying our own necessities in our own country in peace time; in the second place, the control of exports from Canada, and in the third place, the measures that it might be necessary to take if an emergency arose. The first one can be handled in two ways: in the first place, with reference to about eighty per cent of our supplies, where the principle of competition can be utilized one can, I think, safeguard the public interest. But the duty of the government becomes evident when you deal with the remaining ten o.r fifteen or twenty per cent, where the production is highly specialized, and it is in oases such as these that in England they now are using a very rigid system of inspection and of audit, and have introduced the principle of reasonable remuneration, thereby eliminating excessive profits from the production of armaments or munitions. In regard to export to other countries, I think my hon. friends will find, before this session is over, that the provisions of sections 290 and 122 of the Customs Act will be stiffened so as to give the government more control over the export situation.
Has the minister any idea what proportion of this vote is likely to be spent in Canada for the purchase of these supplies? Or will it be spent in England?

Except
with reference to, probably, some guns which could not possibly be made in Canada, by
Supply-Defence-Stores

far the greater proportion, probably eighty per cent, of the amount, will be spent in Canada.
Have any purchases been made or any contracts placed for the purchase of anti-aircraft artillery or heavy guns?
Yes.
If so, from what sources?
I think an order was placed by my predecessor for anti-aircraft guns from England. Of course we are amplifying that order by providing in these estimates for some more anti-aircraft guns.
Could the name of the firm be given?

All orders were placed through the British War Office, as in the case of the Bren guns. I think I probably misled my hon. friends this afternoon. Although those machine guns were made in Czechoslovakia they were ordered through the British War Office.
Are they on trucks or to be put on foundations?

I am
informed that anti-aircraft guns are mobile units.
Have any purchases been made or contracts placed for tanks or armoured motor vehicles?

No; in the estimates we are now considering there is provision for some few light tanks. In the reorganization of the militia which was effected on December 15 last there are six tank battalions created ; each one is to be supplied with one light tank for instructional purposes, and the tank depot at London, Ontario, will have three tanks for instructional purposes.
What purchases have been made or what contracts have been placed for the purchase of machine guns?

Twelve Bren light automatic machine guns, two of which have arrived in Canada, were ordered from the British War Office. There is provision in these estimates for twenty-one more guns of the same kind for instructional uses in the various units throughout Canada; there is also provision for a substantial further number. It has not yet been decided whether they will be obtained from England or manufactured in Canada. An endeavour is being made to see if they can be manufactured here.
What company has secured the manufacturing rights of the Bren gun?
None so far. Several have been endeavouring to do so.
The gun is still under the control of the Czechoslovakian company?
No; the British War Office.
I assume that the government was authorized under previous estimates to place orders for such guns in England?

Yes.
Orders went out last year and the year before.

Do I understand the
minister to say that so far as small arm munitions are concerned, we are in a position to manufacture all our requirements in Canada?

No; I said this, that we are endeavouring through inquiries to find out if we can so do. Last year we certainly did not have the facilities in this country, and as far as I know we do not have them yet. Various people have been endeavouring to obtain the rights for manufacturing machine guns, but so far there is absolutely-
No-small arm munitions. I gathered-and I want to be sure I am correct-that we have facilities in this country to manufacture all the small arm munitions we may require. Is that right?

That is right. We have the facilities here .for manufacturing small arm munitions, and we are providing in these estimates for the augmentation of the productive capacity in the arsenals with reference to small arm munitions.
Small arm munitions are manufactured at the present moment, I suppose, at the arsenal at Quebec?
Yes.
What will the Valcartier arsenal manufacture?
It is another operation of an exactly similar kind to the Quebec arsenal production, an extension of it.

And what about the Lindsay arsenal?

Supply-Defence-Stores
The Lindsay arsenal is at the present time used only for the storage of equipment.
I know that.

The Lindsay arsenal, as my right hon. friend knows, was used for this purpose before and could be so used again. We have made investigations of the cost of so doing. According to the estimates we have received, it would cost $400,000 to place the Lindsay arsenal in a position again to manufacture small arm munitions.
The equipment was not taken away?
No; it was stored there.
And I suppose it is obsolescent as compared with current equipment; is that the position?
Yes.
And those are the three places at which we manufacture small arm munitions?
That is quite correct.
When we come to shell cases, we of course manufactured shell cases in large quantities in this country during the war. Are we in a position to manufacture shell cases in Canada now?

I believe that to a small extent that is now done in the dominion arsenal at Quebec. But my right hon. friend may know that recently a private corporation in Canada is carrying out at Hamilton an order for shell cases for the British government.
Yes. That is the National Steel Car Corporation.

In view of the fact that Lindsay arsenal has been mentioned, I might state that while some of the machinery is obsolete and out of date, a large number of machines are still fit for certain operations.

Speaking this afternoon on item 62, I asked the minister if it was the intention of the department to come every year before parliament or before the committee and ask for such an increase in the vote for national defence. To make my position perfectly clear, I ask the minister if his answer is the same as regards item 63.

Yes; my answer must be the same. I am not in a position at the present time to announce what the
policy of the government may be next year; that must necessarily depend upon conditions then prevailing. However, I should hope that no increases would be necessary. After all, a minister of the crown has responsibilities in connection with his department and I simply could not make, I would refuse to make commitments now with reference to what may be done next year.

If I understood the minister correctly, I understood him to say that the British war department had the right to manufacture certain machine guns, and that certain companies were trying to secure these rights in Canada. Would it be possible for the government to secure them?
Yes, I think so.

I am not inquiring about government policy, but that seems to be the wise course, knowing as I do the minister's attitude towards taking the profits out of war manufacture. Would the government give consideration to such a step?

No decision has been made in that regard, but I want to leave this thought with my hon. friend. In connection with the installation of these factories the preliminary cost is tremendously heavy. The cost of the machinery is heavy, and if in a year's time we could dispense with it there would be an enormous economic change resulting in the throwing out of employment of a good many people. The economic argument must be met. I realize the force of the argument for having these things publicly owned; but if we require some supplies within a reasonable time we may have to cooperate with private interests.

Would not the same argument apply to private concerns? They would have to get equipment, and if it were no longer required the same argument would apply to their staffs, who would no longer be needed.
But it would not cost the private concerns as much.
Why would it cost the government more?
A private concern could turn its plant to a good many other uses.
Are the manufacturers of war material in Canada subsidized?

No, at least not by the Canadian government.
Supply-Defence-Stores
Does this provide for the purchase and use of chemicals in warfare?
No.
No thermite?
No.
Would this be the appropriate item under which to discuss the question of aeroplanes?

That
comes under the next vote, vote No. 69 or No. 70 on page 26.

There is a considerable quantity of machinery stored at Valcartier in storehouses and sheds. I do not remember whether it was for the manufacture of guns or what it was for, but when I inspected the machinery it was all in excellent order, capable of being used again. For what purposes would it foe used?
I am not familiar with that situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That must be the machinery taken from the Ross rifle factory when it was dismantled years ago.
I thought it was in connection with heavy guns.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I believe it has to do with the manufacture of Ross rifles, abandoned since about the middle of the war. That is the machinery now stored in the immigration sheds in Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It has been moved
by Mr. Thorson that item 63 of the estimates of the Department of National Defence be reduced by $3,509,499.
Amendment negatived: yeas, 26; nays, 113.

Will the minister go into a little further detail with regard to this investigation that he is carrying on? I understand that a departmental committee of officers is considering the factory possibilities throughout Canada. How do they know where to go? Are lists submitted? Are applications made, or does the minister send this committee to certain places?

As I
said this afternoon, there was created by order in council an inter-departmental committee from five government departments in connection with an industrial survey in case there might be an emergency, and in the Department of National Defence there has been formed a departmental supply committee called the army, navy and air supply committee. They are making a survey of the

general requirements of the nation industrially. In regard to applications for examination, no application has been refused but in some cases they have not yet completed inspections asked for. Requests have come from public bodies such as boards of trade, firms, from members of parliament and others. As far as I know, in no case has a request been refused. The idea is to make this survey as comprehensive as possible so that there may be on file complete information with reference to all industrial plants in the dominion.
Did the minister publicly intimate that it was desirable to have applications? Is he sure that all factories with possibilities have got into touch with the department?

I do not
believe that was done, and possibly it should be done, because a request came from the committee itself the other day for more publicity in order that all those who are interested may immediately file applications for inspection.

What is the name of the
firm to which the minister referred a minute ago-the firm having contracts with the British government for the manufacture of shellcasing in Canada?

I have
no official knowledge, and can speak only from hearsay, but I believe it was the National Steel Car Corporation of Canada, Limited.

With reference to stores,
to what extent has the minister accepted the advice of experts from the British War Office?
I do not think they were consulted with reference to the stores vote.

Might we have a clearer
explanation of the duties to which these officers have been assigned in Canada? I understand there are twelve. What particular duties have they undertaken in connection with the reorganization of the Canadian military forces. What are the plans for coastal defence?

I do not know of any separate organization in connection with the reorganization. The only organization established is the one I mentioned in reply to the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) with reference to the industrial survey. They have obtained the

Supply-Defence-Stores
services of Colonel Ogilvie of the Department of Mines, but the personnel has not yet been decided upon.
The minister mentioned that in the case of the Bren machine guns, they were obtained through the war office. They were actually manufactured, I think, in Czechoslovakia?
Yes, by the war office.
In connection with the shell cases which were also ordered, or to be ordered through the British War Office, how will that operate? Will they be made in Woolwich?
We have not ordered any so far.
I understood the minister to say they probably would be obtained-[DOT]
No, just ihe few machine guns.

The minister said a moment ago that certain guns were ordered through the British War Office. He mentioned two or three items. What is the modus vivendi in connection with that? How is the British War Office used and what are its functions qua our department?

The first thing, of course, is to get an order in council authorizing the purchase from either the air ministry in regard to certain aeroplanes or the war office, and I think the high commissioner's office in England was used. They are practically acting as agents for the Canadian government in getting supplies for us and thereby assuring us that we are getting good equipment at reasonable prices.

At the present time the British government we understand is working full time and overtime to supply its own requirements. I remember instances when we endeavoured to purchase this and that and found it was impossible to get delivery for two, three or four years. Is the minister not going to run into that difficulty?

Yes, I
quite agree. The average time for the supply of aeroplanes from England is twenty-four months, and it would be longer than that in regard to munitions. I think some equipment ordered by my hon. friend long before he left office has not yet been delivered. That is why it is going to be absolutely necessary for us to supply our own requirements.
That is why I was asking the minister whether or not he believed that this appropriation of $6,000,000 could be spent during the twelve months.
It is going to be very difficult.
Well, it is not for me to suggest what the path of wisdom would be.
The main thing is to get the appropriation through first.
To what extent does this vote provide for the purchase of mines and depth charges for the protection of our harbours and also chains necessary to intercept raiding craft.
There is nothing in this vote. I think there is in the naval vote provision to a certain extent for the equipment mentioned.

The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) asked the minister about ten military officers from Great Britain. They have been mentioned a number of times. Are there ten or twelve, and what are their names and duties?
And experience.

Have we any similar exchanges with other countries?
31111-n



Supply-Defence-Active Militia
No.
Can the minister tell us whether these officers imported from England have been vaccinated?

Item agreed to.
Non-permanent active militia, $2,578,740.
Does this item include disbanded regiments, and, if so, how many?

I think what my hon. friend is referring to is that in the reorganization some of the old regiments have to be disbanded because new units have to be created. There was an increase of artillery units and engineering; some infantry and cavalry units were disbanded, and these were shown on the returns for some time.

I did not catch the minister's answer. I should like to know the definition of a disbanded regiment. Besides that, I wonder whether any of those are considered as non-permanent active militia, or if they will be revived in case of need.
Necessarily a disbanded regiment ceases to exist, but if there should be a change of policy a regiment could be revived with its old name.
A resurrection, in other words.

I thank the minister for his explanation, but may I refer you, sir, to the fact that an hon. gentleman here to-night is an honorary colonel of three disbanded regiments. Most foolish. However, I shall not insist on that. But the minister has just told, us about the officers who have come from England, all captains and one lieutenant, no honorary colonels, no honorary lieutenant-colonels. No one hears of such a thing in Great Britain, but here we like what is fictitious, and we think a lot of these honorary officers. I would ask the minister, for his own peace and security, to drop all appointments of honorary officers. We do not need them. 'Some people are fond of brass hats and so on; I do not care for them, I say that openly and no one will prevent me from saying that I am against brass hats and honorary colonels and honorary lieutenant-colonels. What is most stupid is that there are only two full colonels in active service, and I think forty-six honorary colonels.
Let us be serious. As we have a large country, vast in area, we must have efficient transportation for every unit. May I quote the example of the United States where special officers are trained with great care, possess great skill and will be ready within
[Mr. Coldwell.l
a very brief time to form regiments and battalions. They have the knowledge required of leaders in the army, and with a small group of officers the United States have a very practical non-permanent active militia. I ask the minister whether the officers of his department are aware of the facts as to how the officers are trained at West Point and elsewhere, and whether Canada is to act on similar lines.
May I tell the hon. member that we have the Royal Military 'College, one which is reputed to be as good as any in the United, States or England.

I thank the minister.
Might I ask him the number of officers and men, and their pay, in the non-permanent active militia. While he is looking for the information, may I say that we now see the waste of money in connection with the League of Nations. 'Canada, subscribing to the league, has spent millions of dollars. We are one of the few countries which has honoured bills received from Geneva. What is the result of that? It has been more expense for the Department of National Defence. This is not the only country in that difficulty; every country is in, it. I believe these facts show that the moneys voted for the league are pure waste.

The hon. member for
Temiscouata seems to have a grudge against honorary colonels. May I convey to him the fact that if it were not for some honorary colonels, many of the militia regiments today would not be in existence. The money they get from the government would not keep them long. I know of one honorary colonel who contributed $20,000 in the last two years. They should receive a great deal of credit, and should not be criticized so much.

I thank the hon. member for Parkdale for his kindly interruption. May I ask him how much money the honorary colonel of three disbanded regiments must subscribe to those disbanded regiments to keep them going on, disbanded?
In reply to the hom. member may I say that in the non-permanent militia there are 6,812 officers and 42,080 other ranks, making a total of 48,892 as of June 30, 1936.
How long do the officers and other ranks serve during the year?

As a rule they serve exactly the same length of time. They do their training with their units. In

Supply-Defence

Active Militia
some cases they do their annual training during the summer months. The period of training varies from ten to fourteen days, according to the militia unit concerned.

How many anti-aircraft
batteries are provided in the reorganization?
That has not yet been finally decided upon. The exact location of the anti-aircraft batteries has not yet been decided, but is being considered.
Placing of some of the units has been announced, but I can find no reference to anti-aircraft batteries on the lower mainland of British Columbia. Will a battery be placed there?

This
might come under the heading of coastal defence, as apart from the reorganization of the units of the non-active militia.
Are any militia officers retiring on pension owing to the amalgamation or disbandment of militia units?
No; no officers would be affected, because no pension is payable to non-permanent active militia in that way.

I have heard reference to-night to the pay received by officers of the non-permanent militia. I know a little about what goes on in the non-permanent militia forces, and I have yet to hear of one officer in the non-permanent active militia who has received any of the salary allotted to him. It goes into battalion funds.
Mr. MacNEilL: To what will the increase be devoted?
I want to mention one matter to the minister. Be said that the total number of men in the n'on-active militia was some 48,000. How many were there last year?
Of course the paper strength last year of the militia, before reorganization, was 130,000 in round numbers.
Yes; that is what I am coming to.

The training strength last year was 39,000 in round numbers, and this year we are making provision for a training strength of about 46,000.

Supply-Defence-Active Militia

The point I am trying to make was that when I heard him use the figure the other day I was not unaware of the fact that a report was made to the former government with respect to the matter. Reorganization involved a reduction from 143,000 paper strength to 90,000 paper strength. But paper strength had no value; it was the strength actually on the rolls, and the strength on the rolls last year was a little less than
40.000.	Do I understand the strength on the rolls now is some 48,000?

The
strength on the rolls for training purposes. The paper strength on the rolls this year is about 87,000. We can train only 46,000 of these.
When I use the term "paper strength," I mean the actual men attached to the units. They had 140,000 at one time. That was paper strength, pure and simple.
Yes.

At that time there was a discussion as to the reorganization of eleven divisions with one division of cavalry, as the possible thing. After the Washington conference we reduced that to six divisions with one cavalry division. It is upon that statement the minister is now proceeding with his operations.
It was prior to the disarmament conference, in 1932.

No, no; there were two separate things. I happened to have received the same secret report as the minister is talking about. It provided for eleven divisions, besides the cavalry division. After the Washington conference of 1921-22 we began to readjust our situation. Finally, because of our being called upon to make a report to Geneva for the purposes of the disarmament conference as to what we would regard as our effectives, we made a report which contemplated an effective and paper strength of about
90.000.	I understand it is upon this figure that the minister now proceeds. He contemplates the training of a little more than half that number.
That is right.

The difficulty about the situation is that the paper strength is no indication of the real strength. You can with some degree of certainty say that if you undertake to train 48,000, you probably will be able to train that number. In the breakdown of item number 64, how much is it contemplated to spend on training?
The total amount to be spent on training is $1,785,800.
Is that training for seven days or ten days?
It varies according to the unit. Certain arms of the service get more training, especially the coastal defence batteries and the artillery units.
The infantry training is for seven or ten days?

Artillery, field army, 12 days; coast defence, 21 days. Engineers: units other than fort companies, 12 days; fortress companies, 21 days. R.C.C.S., 14 or 21 days. C.O.T.C., 12 days. Cavalry and infantry, 10 days. R.C.A.S.C. and R.C.A.M.C., 10 days.

I suggest that officers and non-commissioned officers in the non-permanent active militia should be Canadians. A Canadian is more patriotic and makes a better soldier than anyone else and there is no excuse for other than Canadians being in this branch of the service.

I move that vote number 64, non-permanent active militia, be reduced by the amount of $220,640. I move this amendment because of the facts disclosed by the minister during the previous debate. There is every indication that the major part of these appropriations will go to the creation of a mobile force, an ideal arrangement for the dispatch of an expeditionary force overseas. As was intimated, no great attention is being paid to the development of coastal defences or of what might be strictly described as the defence of Canada. There is also every indication of very close cooperation between what has been termed the Canadian war department and the British War Office. I believe our Department of National Defence was rightly described as our war department by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps). We have often suspected that department of being the Canadian branch of the British War Office.
There has been no indication that this department has attempted to achieve any greater efficiency or to overcome the obsolete methods which have been adopted in the past. I directed the attention of the minister to the fact that since the armistice this parliament has voted millions for the purposes of national defence and he has admitted in this house that at the end of that period actually no defence exists, that nothing has been accomplished. The suggestion has been made

Supply-Defence-Active Militia
that we are unchivalrous in attacking the officers of the department, but I would remind the committee that the same practice has been carried out by both sides of the chamber in connection with men who were unable to defend themselves. I think it is quite permissible to question the competency of a department which has shown no results over a long period of years. It is the same staff made up of the same so-called experts *who will be called upon to expend these additional amounts, and there is no definite assurance that under a reorganization the department will achieve a more efficient defence. We have had no assurance from the minister that an adequate plan will be evolved to restrict war profits in advance of the outbreak of war or upon the outbreak of war. There has been no definite assurance from the minister that there will be a proper organization of war industry.
There has been no indication that the department will assume any greater responsibility in the expenditure of these sums in connection with the development of the physiques of the young men who may be called upon to serve in these various units. We may yet be involved in a struggle without any opportunity being given to this house to express the will of the Canadian people. Under the Militia Act as it stands to-day the governor in council may dispatch troops abroad by declaring an emergency, and this would be an accomplished fact when parliament met within fifteen days. they show a distinct politeness to their elders which is lacking in some of those attending our universities.

I had hoped that the minister would answer the very pertinent inquiry made by my hon. friend from Renfrew South. The fact is that I asked the question myself when I first knew of the college. The reason no degrees are awarded is that it is not intended that the college should give a civil education, if I may use that term, and the justification for its existence is found under the head of section 91 of the British North America Act. If it were awarding degrees for academic distinction, it would be placed in such a position that it might be regarded as violating the provisions of section 93 of the British North America Act. It is therefore, a purely constitutional reason why no degrees are awarded. The institution can exist only as a military school. Essentially that characteristic must dominate its life, and if it departs from that and becomes a civil educational institution under the provisions of the provincial legislatures, it can receive no federal aid. That is the real reason.
